vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Update of Pool Split Ratio Enables Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The update_params function allows any governance signer to modify the pool_split_ratio without validating that it does not cause economic imbalance. This ratio directly determines how reward funds are split between balance and weight pools. An attacker can set pool_split_ratio to 0, redirecting 100% of rewards to the weight pool, which can be manipulated by controlling bridge weights. Since weight shares are not capped per bridge in the split_reward logic, an attacker can register a malicious bridge with maximum weight and claim all rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Validation Bypass via Zero L2 Score Exploitation
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_user_reward_script, when l2_score is 0, the merkle proof validation is skipped entirely. An attacker can claim rewards for a bridge by submitting a zero L2 score with empty proofs, even if no valid snapshot exists. This allows claiming rewards for non-existent or manipulated positions. The reward amount is calculated from get_user_funded_reward_internal, which is set by fund_reward_script and can be manipulated by controlling the agent or stage timing.

vulnerabilities.title: Desynchronized Stage Iteration in get_last_submitted_stage Causes Reward Omission
vulnerabilities.description: The get_last_submitted_stage function iterates through stage_data using a table iterator but breaks on the first matching snapshot. However, if a bridge is deregistered and re-registered (creating a new version), the function may skip valid snapshots from older versions because it only checks the first match per stage. This causes operator and user rewards from valid prior stages to be omitted from claimable amounts, permanently locking those funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Weight Pool Reward Calculation Ignores Maximum Weight Ratio After Split
vulnerabilities.description: The calculate_weight_share function correctly caps vip_weight at maximum_weight_ratio, but split_reward_with_share_internal uses the raw share ratio from the SimpleMap without re-applying the cap. If an attacker updates a bridge's vip_weight to exceed maximum_weight_ratio after the weight_shares map is built (e.g., via update_vip_weight), the split_reward function will use the inflated weight ratio to calculate disproportionate rewards, stealing from other bridges.

vulnerabilities.title: Challenge Period Bypass via Time Manipulation in execute_challenge
vulnerabilities.description: The execute_challenge function checks that execution_time < snapshot.create_time + challenge_period, but does not validate that the snapshot was created in a prior stage. An attacker can submit a snapshot with a future create_time (via time manipulation or oracle compromise) and then immediately execute a challenge, bypassing the challenge period entirely. This allows instant override of legitimate snapshots, enabling reward theft by falsifying L2 scores.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Investment via lock_stake_script
vulnerabilities.description: The lock_stake_script function allows users to withdraw vesting rewards and immediately stake them as liquidity, but the function does not verify the source of the funds being withdrawn. An attacker can send funds directly to the VIP contract (e.g., via a bridge or external system) and then trigger lock_stake_script via a maliciously crafted transaction, causing the contract to treat system-returned funds as user-initiated vesting withdrawals. This results in the attacker gaining control over staked liquidity and potentially manipulating TVL and reward distribution calculations.

vulnerabilities.title: Redelegation Hook Uses Stale Share Before for Destination Validator, Leading to Incorrect Locked Share Calculation and Permanent Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: In the redelegate_hook function, when calculating the new locked share for the destination validator, the code uses dst_share_before = current_total_share - redelegation_share.amount. However, redelegation_share.amount is the amount of shares transferred from the source validator, but current_total_share is the total delegation shares after the redelegation has already occurred on-chain. This means dst_share_before represents the total delegation shares before the redelegation, not the shares held by the destination validator before the redelegation. This causes the share_to_locked_share calculation to be incorrect, leading to an overstatement of the locked share deposited at the destination. The overstatement is permanent and results in a mismatch between the on-chain delegation shares and the locked_staking module's accounting. When the user later attempts to undelegate or extend, the system will attempt to withdraw more locked shares than were ever actually delegated, causing the withdraw_delegation function to revert with ENOT_ENOUGH_DELEGATION, permanently locking the user's funds in the staking account without recourse.

vulnerabilities.title: Redelegation Hook Uses Stale Share Before for Accounting, Leading to Incorrect Locked Share Calculation and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The redelegate_hook function calculates the amount of locked shares to withdraw from the source validator using a share_before value passed as a parameter, but this value is not validated against the actual current delegation share on-chain. An attacker can manipulate the share_before value to cause the system to withdraw more locked shares than actually exist, leading to undercounting of locked shares and permanent loss of user funds. The accounting in deposit_delegation then adds the manipulated amount, creating a discrepancy between on-chain delegation shares and the module's locked share tracking.

vulnerabilities.title: Undelegation Hook Uses Stale Share Before for Accounting, Leading to Incorrect Locked Share Calculation and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The undelegate_hook function uses a share_before parameter passed from the caller to calculate the amount of locked shares to withdraw. This value is not validated against the actual current delegation share on-chain. An attacker can pass a manipulated share_before value that is higher than the actual share, causing the system to withdraw more locked shares than exist. This results in undercounting of total_locked_shares and permanent loss of user funds, as the module's accounting becomes inconsistent with the actual staking state.

vulnerabilities.title: Delegate Hook Uses Stale Share Before for Accounting, Leading to Incorrect Locked Share Calculation and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The delegate_hook function uses a share_before parameter passed from the caller to calculate the share difference. This value is not validated against the actual current delegation share on-chain. An attacker can pass a manipulated share_before value that is higher than the actual share, causing the system to calculate a negative or inflated share_diff. This leads to incorrect locked_share calculation and undercounting of total_locked_shares, resulting in permanent loss of user funds when the module's accounting diverges from the actual staking state.

vulnerabilities.title: Redelegation and Undelegation Functions Allow Partial Execution with No Reversion on Failure, Leading to State Inconsistency and Fund Loss
vulnerabilities.description: The redelegate and undelegate functions execute an external stargate call followed by a move_execute hook. If the stargate call succeeds but the move_execute hook fails (e.g., due to gas limits or invalid data), the external state change (redelegate/undelegate) is committed, but the internal accounting (locked shares, total_locked_shares) is not updated. This creates a permanent state inconsistency where the user's locked shares are not reflected in the module's state, effectively locking their funds without proper accounting. There is no mechanism to revert the external call if the hook fails.

vulnerabilities.title: No Minimum Output Protection in Withdraw Functions, Allowing Front-Running and Slashing Exploitation
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw_asset and withdraw_asset_for_staking_account functions allow users to withdraw any amount up to their balance without requiring a minimum output threshold. An attacker can front-run a legitimate withdrawal by triggering a slashing event just before the withdrawal executes. Since the withdrawal amount is fixed and not protected by a minimum output parameter, the user receives less value than expected due to the slashing, with no recourse. This violates Pattern 1: User Control Over Execution Outcomes.

vulnerabilities.title: Validation of Release Time Occurs After External Call in Extend and Batch Extend
vulnerabilities.description: In extend_internal and batch_extend, the release time validation (new_release_time > release_time) occurs before the external call, but the actual delegation withdrawal and deposit happen after. However, the critical flaw is that the validation is performed on the original release_time, but the new_release_time is used in the deposit. If an attacker can manipulate the block time between the validation and the deposit (e.g., via block timestamp manipulation), they can cause the new_release_time to exceed the max_lock_period, but the system will still deposit the delegation because the validation was performed earlier. This allows delegation beyond the max lock period, potentially leading to protocol insolvency if the system cannot handle such long-term liabilities.

vulnerabilities.title: get_exact_provide_amount Function Uses Truncating Multiplication, Leading to Precision Loss and Underpayment in Liquidity Provision
vulnerabilities.description: The get_exact_provide_amount function uses bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate to calculate adjusted coin amounts. This truncates fractional values, leading to precision loss. For example, if the ratio is 1.5 and the amount is 100, the result is 150, but if the ratio is 1.0001 and the amount is 1000000, the result is 1000100 instead of 1000100.0001, losing 0.0001 units. Over many transactions, this accumulates as lost value. The function does not ensure that the total value provided by the user is preserved, violating the principle of fair exchange and leading to gradual loss of user funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Staking Account Creation Allows Front-Running and DoS via Predictable Address Generation
vulnerabilities.description: The get_staking_account_signer function generates a staking account address using object::create_named_object with a seed derived from the user's address and the type name of StakingAccount. This address is deterministic and predictable. An attacker can pre-deploy a contract at this address before the legitimate user does, causing the user's staking account creation to fail. This is a denial-of-service vulnerability that prevents users from participating in the protocol. The function does not check for existing objects at the target address before attempting creation.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in execute_challenge Allows Replay Attacks
vulnerabilities.description: The execute_challenge function commits state changes (updating agent, snapshot, and challenge record) before verifying that the challenge period has expired. This allows an attacker to submit multiple challenges for the same stage, consuming the challenge ID and agent update state even if subsequent challenges fail due to insufficient time elapsed. The state commitment occurs before the external block time check, creating a replay vulnerability.

vulnerabilities.title: Insufficient Validation in batch_claim_user_reward_script Allows Claiming Non-Existent Rewards
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward_script function validates that merkle proofs are correct for non-zero L2 scores, but does not validate that the claimed stage has a corresponding snapshot in the stage_data table. An attacker can submit a valid merkle proof for a non-existent stage (e.g., stage 1000) with zero L2 score, bypassing the merkle proof check entirely and claiming zero reward while consuming a claim slot. This allows denial-of-service by exhausting claimable stages for legitimate users.

vulnerabilities.title: Unbounded Loop in get_last_submitted_stage Causes DoS and Gas Exhaustion
vulnerabilities.description: The get_last_submitted_stage function iterates through all stage_data entries without a bound, searching for a snapshot matching the bridge_id and version. As the number of stages grows (e.g., 1000+), this function becomes prohibitively expensive to call, consuming excessive gas and potentially causing legitimate users to be unable to claim rewards. This is a critical DoS vector since the function is called indirectly by batch_claim_user_reward_script and batch_claim_operator_reward_script.

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent Reward Calculation in split_reward_with_share_internal Uses Truncated Multiplication
vulnerabilities.description: The split_reward_with_share_internal function uses bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate, which truncates fractional results. When multiple bridges are involved, the sum of truncated rewards can be less than the total reward allocated, causing protocol insolvency. For example, with total_reward = 1000, two bridges each with 0.6 share: each gets 600 (0.6 * 1000 = 600), but 600 + 600 = 1200 > 1000. However, if shares are 0.4 and 0.4, each gets 400, totaling 800, leaving 200 unallocated. This creates a systematic loss of funds over time.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Access Control in update_agent_by_chain Allows Unauthorized Agent Changes
vulnerabilities.description: The update_agent_by_chain function allows any chain signer to change the protocol agent, but the check_chain_permission function only verifies the chain address, not the governance authority. Since chain addresses are publicly known and can be spoofed or controlled by malicious actors, this function effectively allows any entity to take over the protocol's agent, enabling theft of funds, manipulation of snapshots, and disruption of reward distribution.

vulnerabilities.title: State Synchronization Failure in fund_reward_script Causes Reward Miscalculation
vulnerabilities.description: In fund_reward_script, the function calls add_tvl_snapshot_internal twice: once before incrementing stage and once after. The second call uses the new stage value, but the reward calculation (vault::reward_per_stage()) is based on the old state. This causes the reward amount to be calculated using outdated TVL data, leading to incorrect reward distribution. For example, if TVL increases between the two calls, the reward is calculated on the lower TVL, underpaying users and overpaying operators.

vulnerabilities.title: Insecure Merkle Proof Verification in assert_merkle_proofs Allows Forgery
vulnerabilities.description: The assert_merkle_proofs function assumes sorted merkle proofs and uses a simple left/right concatenation to reconstruct the root. However, it does not validate that the proof path is valid for the target hash. An attacker can submit a proof that is a concatenation of two arbitrary hashes that happen to hash to the correct root, bypassing the proof validation. This allows forging L2 scores and claiming rewards for non-existent positions.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Parameter Updates Allow Protocol Insolvency via Pool Split Ratio Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The update_params function allows governance to set pool_split_ratio to any value between 0 and 1, but does not validate that the sum of pool_split_ratio and weight_ratio (1 - pool_split_ratio) equals 1 in accounting. If an attacker gains governance control and sets pool_split_ratio to 0.999, then weight_pool_reward_amount becomes 0.001 * initial_reward_amount. This causes 99.9% of rewards to go to the balance pool, but if the weight pool is the only one with valid snapshots, users receive almost nothing, leading to protocol insolvency and loss of user trust.

vulnerabilities.title: Automatic Processing of Withdrawal Funds Triggers Unintended Investment
vulnerabilities.description: The contract's withdraw_asset_for_staking_account function automatically withdraws uinit rewards from the staking account after every delegation, redelegate, and undelegate operation. Since uinit is a native token that can be sent to the staking account address, an attacker can send uinit to the staking account address during a withdrawal operation, causing the system to automatically process it as a new deposit via the hook functions. This creates a loop where system-returned funds (uinit) are treated as user deposits, leading to double-counting of assets and inflation of the protocol's total locked value.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Validation Bypass Due to Zero L2 Score Handling
vulnerabilities.description: The function `assert_merkle_proofs` skips Merkle proof validation when `l2_score == 0`, but `batch_claim_user_reward_script` still allows claiming rewards for zero L2 score entries. This creates a critical vulnerability where an attacker can claim rewards for non-existent or zero-score positions by submitting empty Merkle proofs, effectively minting free rewards. The reward calculation uses `get_user_funded_reward_internal` which returns a positive value even if the Merkle proof was never validated, leading to unauthorized fund extraction.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Distribution Miscalculation Due to Truncation in BigDecimal Multiplication
vulnerabilities.description: The function `split_reward_with_share_internal` uses `bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate` to calculate reward shares. This truncates fractional values, causing systematic underpayment to bridges over time. When multiple bridges claim rewards across stages, the truncated fractions accumulate, leading to a permanent loss of funds that are never distributed. For example, with a 100,000,000,000 reward and 10 bridges each with 1/10 weight, each should receive 10,000,000,000. But if the BigDecimal multiplication truncates 0.999... to 9,999,999,999 per bridge, 10 bridges lose 10,000,000,000 total over 100 stages — a 10% loss of total rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent Stage Validation in `check_previous_stage_snapshot` Allows Stage Skipping
vulnerabilities.description: The function `check_previous_stage_snapshot` checks for a previous stage snapshot only if `stage != init_stage`. However, if a bridge is deregistered and re-registered, its `init_stage` is set to the current stage + 1. An attacker can deregister a bridge, wait for the next stage, then re-register it with a new version, effectively resetting its `init_stage`. This allows the attacker to submit a snapshot for stage N without validating the snapshot for stage N-1, bypassing the entire historical chain of proof. This enables fabrication of L2 scores and reward claims for non-existent historical data.

vulnerabilities.title: Operator Reward Claiming Bypasses Challenge Period Check
vulnerabilities.description: The function `batch_claim_operator_reward_script` does not verify `is_after_challenge_period` before allowing operator reward claims. While user rewards require challenge period validation, operator rewards are claimed immediately after the last submitted stage, regardless of whether the challenge period has elapsed. This allows an operator to claim rewards for a stage immediately after submitting a snapshot, before any challenge can be raised, effectively eliminating the challenge mechanism for operators and enabling front-running of reward claims.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted `update_agent` Allows Unauthorized Agent Takeover
vulnerabilities.description: The function `update_agent` requires only the current agent's signature to change the protocol agent. However, `update_agent_by_chain` allows any chain signer to change the agent. Since `utils::check_chain_permission` is not verified to be a trusted system account, an attacker who gains access to any chain signer (e.g., via compromised validator) can call `update_agent_by_chain` to replace the agent with a malicious address. This grants full control over reward funding, snapshot submission, and challenge execution, leading to complete protocol compromise.

vulnerabilities.title: Vesting Period Update Allows Reward Theft via Shortened Vesting
vulnerabilities.description: The `update_vesting_period` function allows governance to reduce the vesting period. When the vesting period is shortened, the function `vesting::batch_claim_user_reward` recalculates vesting amounts based on the new period. However, the initial reward amount stored in `UserVestingClaimInfo` is not adjusted. An attacker can wait for a high-reward stage, then vote to reduce the vesting period from 26 to 1. When users claim, they receive the full initial reward amount in one claim instead of being distributed over 26 stages — effectively stealing 25/26 of the intended future rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Root Reuse Across Versions Enables Replay Attacks
vulnerabilities.description: The `SnapshotKey` uses only `bridge_id` and `version` but does not include the `stage` in its key. When a bridge is deregistered and re-registered with the same `bridge_id` but a new `version`, the `snapshots` table is reused. An attacker can submit a valid Merkle proof from a previous version's stage and reuse it for the new version's stage, because the snapshot lookup does not distinguish between versions and stages. This allows replay of old snapshots to claim rewards for new stages without valid L2 data.

vulnerabilities.title: Maximum TVL Ratio Applied Incorrectly in Balance Share Calculation
vulnerabilities.description: In `calculate_balance_share`, the maximum effective balance is calculated as `max_effective_balance = maximum_tvl_ratio * total_balance`. However, this cap is applied per bridge, but the share calculation uses `effective_bridge_balance / total_balance`. If one bridge has a TVL above the cap, its share is capped, but the total_balance used in the denominator still includes the full (uncapped) TVL of all bridges. This causes the sum of all shares to be less than 1.0, meaning a portion of the reward pool is permanently lost. For example, with 2 bridges each at 100% of max_tvl_ratio, total_balance = 200, max_effective = 100, each bridge gets 100/200 = 0.5, sum = 1.0 — correct. But if one bridge has 150 and the other 50, total_balance = 200, max_effective = 100, shares = 100/200 + 50/200 = 0.75 — 25% of reward is lost.

vulnerabilities.title: Precision Loss in share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share Due to Integer Division Truncation
vulnerabilities.description: The functions share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share perform financial conversions using integer division (bigdecimal::div) without proper rounding or overflow protection. When converting between shares and locked shares, the formula (share * total_locked_share) / total_share can truncate fractional values, leading to permanent loss of funds over multiple operations. This occurs because BigDecimal division in Move truncates toward zero, and the protocol does not accumulate or compensate for these losses. Over time, repeated delegations, redelegations, and extensions cause users to lose small fractions of their stake, which accumulate to significant amounts.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Completion in Redelegate and Undelegate
vulnerabilities.description: In both redelegate and undelegate entry functions, state changes (withdraw_delegation) are performed before the external stargate call. If the stargate call reverts (e.g., due to network congestion, validator downtime, or malicious behavior), the local state has already been modified (delegation removed), but the on-chain staking operation failed. This results in a permanent state inconsistency: the user's locked delegation is removed from the local table, but no corresponding on-chain redelegation or undelegation occurred. The user loses access to their stake without any on-chain record of the action.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - State Commitment Timing

vulnerabilities.title: Authorization Context Not Bound in Hook Functions Leading to Front-Running
vulnerabilities.description: The hook functions (delegate_hook, redelegate_hook, undelegate_hook) are called after stargate transactions but use the staking account signer as context. However, the authorization (signature or access control) is not bound to the specific parameters of the operation (e.g., validator, amount, release_time). An attacker can observe a legitimate transaction, front-run it with a malicious transaction using the same staking account signer, and change the validator or release_time in the hook call. Since the hook only validates the signer and not the operation context, the attacker can redirect rewards or extend lock periods maliciously.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Authorization Context Binding

vulnerabilities.title: Fork Behavioral Divergence: Querying /initia.mstaking.v1.Query/Redelegations on Non-Initia Chains
vulnerabilities.description: The contract assumes the existence of the stargate query path '/initia.mstaking.v1.Query/Redelegations' and its response structure. However, if this module is deployed on a forked chain (e.g., a Cosmos SDK chain not based on Initia), this endpoint may not exist or may return a different structure (e.g., with pagination, multiple entries, or different field names). The contract asserts vector length == 1 and expects specific fields (creation_height, shares_dst), which will cause the transaction to revert on incompatible chains. This breaks the entire redelegation functionality on non-Initia forks without warning.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: External Integration Integrity - Fork Behavioral Divergence

vulnerabilities.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in bigdecimal::div Without Zero Check
vulnerabilities.description: The function share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share use bigdecimal::div to compute (share * total_locked_share) / total_share. However, there is no validation that total_share != 0 before division. If total_share is zero (e.g., due to a race condition or initial state), the division by zero results in undefined behavior. In Move's BigDecimal implementation, this may cause a panic or return an invalid value (e.g., NaN or infinity), which then propagates into locked_share calculations. This can lead to incorrect delegation amounts, denial of service, or fund locking.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Type System Integrity - Mathematical Domain Validation

vulnerabilities.title: Incomplete State Restoration in Extend Operation
vulnerabilities.description: The extend operation withdraws the old delegation and deposits a new one with a new release_time. However, the total_locked_shares table is updated correctly, but the delegations table is not properly cleaned up if the old delegation key is reused. The function withdraw_delegation removes the old key, but if the new delegation uses the same validator and metadata but different release_time, the old key is deleted and the new one is added. However, if the new release_time is the same as the old one (due to user error or front-running), the old key is removed and a new one is added, but the total_locked_shares is incremented twice — once in withdraw and once in deposit — leading to double-counting of locked shares and potential over-allocation of rewards.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Operation Reversal Completeness

vulnerabilities.title: Voting Power Recalculation After Vote Does Not Update Tally, Leading to Undercounting and Fund Misallocation
vulnerabilities.description: The protocol allows users to update their votes during a voting period, but when a user changes their vote, the system correctly removes the old vote's contribution from the tally but fails to account for the fact that the user's total voting power may have changed between the original vote and the updated vote. This causes the new vote's contribution to be calculated using the current (possibly higher) voting power, while the old vote was removed using the old voting power. This creates a net gain in total tally that is not backed by actual voting power, enabling attackers to manipulate proposal outcomes by strategically timing vote updates when their voting power increases due to external factors (e.g., new staking, vesting cliff). The mathematical error leads to inflation of total tally, misallocating weight to bridges and potentially allowing malicious actors to control governance outcomes with less actual stake.
vulnerabilities.location: vote() function, lines 180-210; remove_vote() and apply_vote() functions

vulnerabilities.title: Representation Boundary Violation in Locked Share to Amount Conversion
vulnerabilities.description: The function locked_share_to_amount incorrectly assumes that the total_share and total_locked_share are in the same unit scale when converting locked shares to amounts. This leads to a miscalculation of the actual staked amount after slashing events, causing users to receive incorrect amounts upon withdrawal. The issue arises because locked_share_to_amount uses share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share, which perform proportional calculations based on total_locked_share and total_share, but these values are not consistently scaled. When slashing occurs, the mstaking module reduces the balance (amount) but keeps the shares constant. However, the lock_staking module's share_to_locked_share function assumes the total_share reflects the post-slash value, when in reality it still reflects the pre-slash value. This causes locked_share_to_amount to overstate the amount corresponding to a locked share, leading to users withdrawing more than they are entitled to after slashing events.

vulnerabilities.title: Access Control Violation in update_params Function
vulnerabilities.description: The update_params function allows any signer with chain permission to modify critical economic parameters (min_lock_period, max_lock_period, max_delegation_slot) without any timelock or multi-sig requirement. An attacker with temporary chain permission (e.g., via compromised validator or governance exploit) can set max_lock_period to 0, effectively disabling all lock-up periods. This allows users to immediately withdraw staked assets after delegation, bypassing the entire locking mechanism. The economic impact is catastrophic: users can stake, immediately withdraw, and repeat this cycle to drain the protocol's liquidity without any time-based risk. The function lacks any access control beyond utils::check_chain_permission, which is insufficient for parameters that directly govern economic security.

vulnerabilities.title: Data Collection Integrity Failure in get_locked_delegations Iteration
vulnerabilities.description: The get_locked_delegations function iterates over delegations using a table iterator but uses a SimpleMap to cache delegation responses. However, if a delegation is removed during iteration (e.g., via redelegate or undelegate triggered by another transaction), the SimpleMap may contain stale or incomplete data. The function assumes that the validator-to-delegation mapping is static during iteration, but in reality, the underlying delegations table can be modified by concurrent operations. This creates a race condition where the returned vector of LockedDelegationResponse may miss valid delegations or include invalid ones. For example, if a user redeploys from validator A to B during iteration, the delegation to A may be removed from the delegations table but the SimpleMap still holds the old delegation response, causing the function to return an incorrect count of delegations. This can lead to incorrect reward calculations and withdrawal amounts.

vulnerabilities.title: Representation Boundary Violation in share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share
vulnerabilities.description: The functions share_to_locked_share and locked_share_to_share perform proportional conversions between shares and locked shares using total_share and total_locked_share, but these values are not consistently updated after slashing events. When slashing occurs, the mstaking module reduces the balance (amount) but keeps the shares constant. However, the lock_staking module's total_locked_shares table is never updated to reflect the reduced value of shares after slashing. This causes share_to_locked_share to overstate the locked share value because it assumes the total_share still represents the full pre-slash value. For example, if a user has 100 shares and total_share is 1000, and slashing reduces the underlying asset value by 10%, the actual value of 100 shares is now 90, but the lock_staking module still calculates locked_share = (100 * total_locked_share) / 1000, ignoring the 10% reduction. This leads to users withdrawing 10% more than they should after slashing events.

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent Unit Handling in redelegate_hook and undelegate_hook
vulnerabilities.description: The redelegate_hook and undelegate_hook functions use the share_before parameter passed from the external transaction, but this value is not validated against the actual current share state in the mstaking module. The functions assume that the share_before value provided by the caller is accurate, but an attacker can manipulate this value to be artificially high. For example, in redelegate_hook, if the attacker provides a share_before value that is 10x higher than the actual pre-redelegate share, the function will calculate a negative share_diff and incorrectly withdraw a large amount of locked share from the source validator. This allows the attacker to drain locked shares from the source validator and deposit them to the destination validator without actually having those shares, effectively creating new shares out of thin air. The same issue exists in undelegate_hook.

vulnerabilities.title: Vote Power Recalculation After Vote Removal Leads to Double Counting and Protocol Insolvency
vulnerabilities.description: The vote() function removes a user's previous vote and subtracts its weight from the proposal's tallies, but then applies the new vote and adds its weight. However, the voting_power_used is calculated from the new weights and max_voting_power, while the removal uses the old weights. This creates a window where the total_tally is temporarily reduced and then increased, but the accounting is inconsistent if the user's max_voting_power changes between the removal and application phases. An attacker can exploit this by triggering a vote removal and then a new vote in the same transaction while manipulating their voting power via external state changes (e.g., lock staking expiration or vesting claim), causing the protocol to overcount voting power and distribute disproportionate weights to bridges, leading to permanent misallocation of governance power and potential theft of protocol-controlled assets.

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before Operation Verification in Vote Processing
vulnerabilities.description: The vote() function modifies the proposal's total_tally and bridge-specific tallies before verifying that the vote weights sum to exactly 1.0. This allows an attacker to submit a vote with weights summing to less than 1.0, receive proportional voting power, and then submit a second vote with the same weights (or different) to reclaim the previously subtracted voting power, effectively double-spending voting power. The vulnerability arises because the remove_vote() function subtracts the old vote's contribution from tallies before the new vote is applied, but the new vote's weights are not validated for exact sum=1.0 until after the state has been modified.

vulnerabilities.title: Precision Loss in BigDecimal Multiplication Truncates Voting Power
vulnerabilities.description: The code uses bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate() to compute voting power from weights and amounts, which truncates fractional results. This causes systematic undercounting of voting power when weights are fractional, leading to incorrect tally calculations. The truncation is not compensated for, and the same vote can yield different results if the underlying amounts change due to external events (e.g., slashing or delegation changes), even if the weight vector remains identical.

vulnerabilities.title: State Inconsistency in Vote Update Due to Incomplete Tally Restoration
vulnerabilities.description: When a user updates their vote, the system removes the previous vote via remove_vote() and applies the new one via apply_vote(). However, remove_vote() subtracts the old voting power from proposal.total_tally, but does not reset the individual bridge tallies to zero before applying the new vote. This creates a race condition where if two users update votes simultaneously, the intermediate state may temporarily overcount or undercount total_tally. More critically, if a vote is removed and then re-applied with the same weights, the total_tally may be incorrectly adjusted due to truncation errors accumulating across multiple updates.

vulnerabilities.title: Voting Power Calculation Ignores Sign Bit in BigDecimal Operations
vulnerabilities.description: The code assumes all BigDecimal values are non-negative (e.g., weights, multipliers, amounts). However, the BigDecimal implementation in initia_std may support negative values. If a malicious actor can manipulate the pair_multipliers table to store a negative weight (e.g., via a compromised admin or reentrancy), the multiplication and addition in get_voting_power() will produce mathematically invalid results. The system does not validate that weights or multipliers are positive before use, violating the mathematical domain requirement for voting power aggregation.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Type System Integrity - Mathematical Domain Validation

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call in execute_proposal_internal
vulnerabilities.description: The execute_proposal_internal() function commits state (proposal.executed = true) before calling vip::update_vip_weights_for_friend(). If the external call to vip::update_vip_weights_for_friend() reverts (e.g., due to gas limits, invalid bridge IDs, or contract upgrade), the proposal is still marked as executed, preventing any future vote or update on that cycle. This leaves the system in a permanently inconsistent state where votes are frozen but weights are not updated, effectively locking governance.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - State Commitment Timing

vulnerabilities.title: Fork Behavioral Divergence in vip::update_vip_weights_for_friend
vulnerabilities.description: The code assumes vip::update_vip_weights_for_friend() updates the core voting weight registry. However, if the VIP protocol has been forked (e.g., to move weight management to a separate contract like a 'WeightDistributor'), this function may no longer perform any state change. The proposal is marked as executed and an event is emitted, but the actual weights used in the protocol remain unchanged. This results in governance votes being tallied correctly but never applied, causing funds and voting power to be misallocated indefinitely.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: External Integration Integrity - Fork Behavioral Divergence

vulnerabilities.title: Incorrect Reward Calculation in batch_claim_previous_user_vestings Due to Zero Division and Missing Penalty Accounting
vulnerabilities.description: In the batch_claim_previous_user_vestings function, when calculating vest_amount based on l2_score and minimum_score, if minimum_score is zero, the multiplication and division (utils::mul_div_u64) will result in zero reward even if l2_score > 0. This causes users to lose all vested rewards when minimum_score == 0, despite having non-zero L2 scores. Additionally, penalty_reward is only incremented when vest_amount < vest_max_amount, but when minimum_score == 0, vest_amount becomes 0, and the penalty is incorrectly calculated as vest_max_amount, but this penalty is never properly tracked or returned to the user. The function also fails to emit a UserVestingFinalizedEvent with the correct penalty_reward when the vesting is finalized due to minimum_score == 0, leading to permanent loss of penalty rewards and incorrect accounting. This is a critical economic manipulation vulnerability that allows protocol operators to effectively confiscate user rewards by setting minimum_score = 0.

vulnerabilities.title: Unchecked Vote Removal Leads to Double-Spending of Voting Power
vulnerabilities.description: The vote() function allows users to update their votes by removing their previous vote and applying a new one. However, when removing a previous vote, the function subtracts the voting power from the proposal's total_tally and bridge tallies, but it does not validate that the previously stored voting power matches the current calculated voting power. This allows an attacker to manipulate the voting power calculation by changing their underlying staking or vesting positions between vote submissions, causing the system to subtract an incorrect amount and then add a new amount, effectively creating free voting power. This is a critical representation boundary violation where the system assumes voting power is immutable between votes, but it is dynamically calculated from external state (lock_staking, vesting, mstaking) that can change at any time.
vulnerabilities.location: vote() function, lines 185-205 and remove_vote() function, lines 255-268

vulnerabilities.title: Voting Power Calculation Uses Dynamic External State Without Snapshots
vulnerabilities.description: The get_voting_power() function calculates a user's voting power by querying live external state from lock_staking, vesting, and mstaking. However, this value is used as a static snapshot in vote() when a user casts a vote. Since these external systems can change between the time get_voting_power() is called and when the vote is processed (e.g., via undelegation, claim, or lock expiration), the voting power used in vote() is not a consistent snapshot. This creates a representation boundary violation: the vote() function expects a stable unit of voting power for accounting, but receives a dynamic value. An attacker can time their vote to coincide with a moment of artificially inflated voting power (e.g., just before undelegating), then immediately undelegate to reduce their stake, effectively gaining disproportionate voting influence without proportional stake.
vulnerabilities.location: get_voting_power() function, lines 300-350; vote() function, line 175

vulnerabilities.title: Proposal Execution Uses Whitelisted Bridge IDs Instead of Active Votes
vulnerabilities.description: The execute_proposal_internal() function retrieves bridge weights using vip::get_whitelisted_bridge_ids(), which returns all registered bridges. However, the proposal's tallies only contain entries for bridges that received votes. When calculating weights, the function divides each bridge's tally by total_tally and assigns a weight even if the bridge received zero votes. This creates a representation boundary violation: the function assumes all whitelisted bridges should be represented in the output, but the economic model only assigns weight to bridges that received votes. This causes dilution of voting power: bridges with zero votes receive non-zero weights, reducing the weight of bridges that actually received votes. This is a data access integrity issue where the iteration mechanism (all whitelisted bridges) is desynchronized from the actual data (only voted bridges have tallies).

vulnerabilities.title: Voting Power Truncation in BigDecimal Operations Causes Systematic Undercounting
vulnerabilities.description: The code uses bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate() to convert voting power into weighted votes. This function truncates fractional values, meaning every multiplication loses precision. Since voting power is calculated as a sum of multiple truncated values (from mstaking, lock_staking, vesting), and then multiplied again by weights (which are also BigDecimal), the cumulative truncation error is significant and systematic. For example, if a user has 1000 voting power and votes with weights [0.5, 0.5], each bridge gets 500. But if the user has 1001 voting power, each bridge gets 500 (truncated), losing 1 unit. Over many users and votes, this creates a systematic undercounting of total voting power. The total_tally becomes less than the sum of all individual voting powers, leading to underweighting of bridges and potential insolvency of the voting system over time.
vulnerabilities.location: apply_vote() and remove_vote() functions, lines 260-267 and 257-264; get_voting_power() function, lines 310, 325, 335

vulnerabilities.title: No Access Control on create_proposal() Enables Timing Attacks on Cycle Initialization
vulnerabilities.description: The create_proposal() function is publicly callable and updates critical economic state: current_cycle, cycle_start_time, cycle_end_time, and creates a new proposal with a voting_end_time. An attacker can call create_proposal() at any time to force a new cycle, effectively shortening the voting period for the next proposal. Since the voting period is fixed (e.g., 80 seconds) and the cycle interval is fixed (e.g., 100 seconds), an attacker can trigger a new cycle just before the natural end of the current cycle, reducing the voting window from 80 seconds to as little as 1 second. This allows the attacker to manipulate the outcome of proposals by preventing legitimate voters from participating, effectively enabling a denial-of-service attack on governance participation.

vulnerabilities.title: Desynchronized Iteration in batch_claim_user_reward Leads to Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward function extracts user vestings into a vector, then iterates over claim_infos to process vesting claims. During this iteration, it calls batch_claim_previous_user_vestings, which modifies the same vector by removing finalized vestings. However, the outer loop continues to iterate over the original claim_infos vector while the inner function modifies the vestings vector in-place. Crucially, the last_claimed_stage variable is updated per claim_info, but the vestings vector is being shrunk during iteration. This creates a desynchronization between the claim_info index and the actual vesting data structure. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a claim_info with a very high start_stage value early in the vector, causing earlier vestings to be finalized and removed from the vector. Subsequent claim_infos may then reference vesting positions that no longer exist in the vector, causing the batch_claim_previous_user_vestings function to skip processing them entirely. This results in unclaimed rewards being permanently lost or misallocated, effectively allowing the attacker to steal rewards intended for other users by manipulating the order of claim_infos.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Access Control on User Vesting Creation Enables Reward Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The create_user_vesting function is called by batch_claim_user_reward, which is marked public(friend) and can be invoked by any entity with access to the VIP module. However, there is no access control verifying that the caller is authorized to create vesting positions for a given user. An attacker can call batch_claim_user_reward with fabricated UserVestingClaimInfo entries for any user address, creating vesting positions with arbitrary initial_reward values. Since the vault::withdraw(total_vested_reward) at the end of batch_claim_user_reward transfers real funds based on the sum of these fabricated rewards, the attacker can mint unlimited rewards for themselves by claiming on a user address they control, effectively draining the vault. This is a direct economic manipulation vulnerability where the attacker controls the input to a state-updating function that directly affects fund distribution.

vulnerabilities.title: Unit Mismatch in L2 Score Calculation Causes Underpayment of Rewards
vulnerabilities.description: The function batch_claim_user_reward calculates initial_reward_amount using utils::mul_div_u64(total_user_reward, claim_info.l2_score, claim_info.total_l2_score). However, the UserVesting struct stores l2_score and minimum_score as u64, while minimum_score_ratio is a BigDecimal. The minimum_score is calculated as bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate(claim_info.minimum_score_ratio, claim_info.l2_score), which truncates precision. Later, in batch_claim_previous_user_vestings, the vest_amount is calculated as utils::mul_div_u64(value.vest_max_amount, claim_info.l2_score, value.minimum_score). This creates a cascading unit mismatch: the numerator (l2_score) is a raw u64, but the denominator (minimum_score) is a truncated BigDecimal result. This causes the division to be inaccurate, systematically underpaying users when their l2_score is not a multiple of the minimum_score_ratio. For example, if total_l2_score=1000, funded_reward=1000, and a user has l2_score=1, minimum_score_ratio=0.001 (1e-3), then minimum_score=1. The calculation yields 1000 * 1 / 1000 = 1, which is correct. But if minimum_score_ratio=0.000999 (999e-6), then minimum_score=0 (truncated), causing division by zero or incorrect scaling. This results in users receiving 0 reward when they should receive a fraction, leading to permanent underpayment and loss of user funds.

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent Last Claimed Stage Update Enables Double Claiming
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_user_reward, last_claimed_stage is initialized to 0 and updated inside the vector::for_each_ref loop over claim_infos. However, if the first claim_info has start_stage=5, last_claimed_stage becomes 5. But if the second claim_info has start_stage=3 (which is less than 5), the function still proceeds because it only checks table::contains for the specific stage key, not whether the stage is monotonically increasing. The update_user_last_claimed_stage is called only once at the end with the last value of last_claimed_stage (which is the final claim_info's start_stage). This means if an attacker submits claim_infos in descending order of start_stage (e.g., [10, 5, 3]), the last_claimed_stage will be set to 3, even though vesting positions at stages 5 and 10 were already claimed. This allows the same user to submit another batch_claim_user_reward with claim_infos [3, 4, 5] and re-claim rewards for stages 3, 4, 5 — because the last_claimed_stage was incorrectly set to 3, not 10. This enables double claiming of the same reward positions, leading to inflation of user rewards and theft from the vault.

vulnerabilities.title: Withdrawal Funds Re-processed as New Deposits via batch_claim_user_reward
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward function processes user vesting claims and withdraws funds from the vault. However, if an attacker sends funds directly to the vesting contract (e.g., via a bridge or external system), those funds are indistinguishable from legitimate withdrawal returns. The contract's withdrawal mechanism (vault::withdraw) returns funds to the caller, but the batch_claim_user_reward function does not verify the source of funds. This allows an attacker to trigger batch_claim_user_reward with a claim_info that has zero funded_reward, causing the function to emit UserVestingCreateEvent with 0 reward, but then the vault::withdraw(total_vested_reward) call returns funds to the attacker — effectively allowing the attacker to claim back any funds sent to the contract as if they were legitimate rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Reward Withdrawal Allows Arbitrary Fund Extraction
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw function allows any caller to withdraw any amount of funds from the vault as long as reward_per_stage > 0, with no validation against deposited balance or caller authorization. This enables an attacker to drain the entire vault balance by repeatedly calling withdraw() with large amounts, even if they never deposited any funds. The function uses a signer generated from the module's extend_ref, which is accessible to anyone, and does not check if the requested withdrawal amount exceeds the available balance in the vault store. This breaks the fundamental invariant that withdrawals must be bounded by available reserves.
vulnerabilities.location: fun withdraw(amount: u64): FungibleAsset acquires ModuleStore { ... }

vulnerabilities.title: State Synchronization Failure in batch_claim_user_reward Leads to Double Claiming and Fund Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward function extracts user vestings into a local vector, processes claims on the vector, then attempts to re-synchronize the table with the modified vector. However, during the processing loop, the function calls batch_claim_previous_user_vestings which modifies the vector in-place and removes finalized vestings. After the loop, the function iterates over the vector and calls table::upsert on each vesting, but does not clear the original table first. This causes vestings that were removed from the vector (because they were finalized) to be re-inserted into the table if they were not overwritten by a later upsert, leading to duplicate vesting entries. An attacker can exploit this by triggering multiple batch claims with overlapping stages, causing the same vesting to be claimed multiple times and withdrawing the same reward multiple times from the vault.

vulnerabilities.title: Division by Zero in User Reward Calculation Allows Full Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_user_reward, the function calculates initial_reward_amount using utils::mul_div_u64(total_user_reward, claim_info.l2_score, claim_info.total_l2_score). If claim_info.total_l2_score is 0, the function correctly sets initial_reward_amount to 0. However, in batch_claim_previous_user_vestings, the function calculates vest_amount using utils::mul_div_u64(value.vest_max_amount, claim_info.l2_score, value.minimum_score). If value.minimum_score is 0 (which can occur if claim_info.minimum_score_ratio is 0 or l2_score is 0), this division by zero will cause the transaction to abort. But if the minimum_score is computed as 0 via bigdecimal::mul_by_u64_truncate (which truncates and can return 0 even if inputs are non-zero), and claim_info.l2_score > 0, then the division by zero occurs during claim processing. This allows an attacker to construct a claim_info with minimum_score_ratio = 0 and l2_score > 0, causing the transaction to abort during claim processing. However, because the function does not revert the entire batch on partial failure, and because the initial_reward_amount is set to 0 for that stage, the attacker can claim the funded_reward as 0, but the underlying vesting remains in the table. Later, when the vesting is claimed again with a different claim_info, the same vesting can be claimed again, leading to double-spending of the same reward.

vulnerabilities.title: Missing User Protection in batch_claim_user_reward Allows Manipulation of Reward Distribution
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward function allows an external actor to submit a vector of UserVestingClaimInfo that determines how much reward is allocated to each vesting stage. There is no mechanism for the user to specify a minimum acceptable reward output per stage or overall. An attacker can submit a malicious claim_info vector that artificially inflates the total_l2_score while minimizing individual l2_score values, causing utils::mul_div_u64 to round down to 0 for all vestings, resulting in 0 reward being distributed to the user even though the funded_reward is non-zero. The user has no way to reject this execution or set a floor on acceptable output. This is a violation of Pattern 1: User Control Over Execution Outcomes. The user's entire reward can be stolen by a malicious actor submitting a claim_info vector with manipulated total_l2_score.

vulnerabilities.title: Validation After State Change in withdraw_vesting Allows Unauthorized Withdrawals
vulnerabilities.description: In withdraw_vesting, the function first retrieves the UserVesting from the table, then checks if user_vesting.remaining_reward >= withdraw_amount. However, the state change (user_vesting.remaining_reward -= withdraw_amount) occurs before any validation of the caller's authority. The function does not verify that the caller is the owner of the account_addr. This means any actor can call withdraw_vesting with any account_addr and stage, and if they know the stage key, they can withdraw any portion of the remaining reward. This is a clear violation of Pattern 2: Validation Timing. Validation occurs after state change, allowing unauthorized state modification. An attacker can withdraw funds from any user's vesting position if they can guess or obtain the stage key.

vulnerabilities.title: Inconsistent State Update in batch_claim_operator_reward Causes Reward Underpayment and Loss
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_operator_reward, the function iterates over operator vestings using utils::walk_mut and calculates vested_amount based on last_submitted_stage. However, the total_vested_reward is accumulated inside the walk_mut closure, but the function does not validate that the calculated reward_amount is non-negative. If last_submitted_stage < operator_vesting.start_stage, then stage_diff is negative, and utils::mul_div_u64 returns 0, so reward_amount becomes 0 - vested_amount = -vested_amount. Since u64 cannot be negative, this underflow causes a transaction abort. But if the underflow is avoided by design (e.g., if stage_diff is clamped to 0), then reward_amount becomes 0, and the operator's remaining_reward is decremented by 0, meaning the operator never receives any reward for stages that have not yet started. This leads to permanent loss of operator rewards. The function does not validate that last_submitted_stage >= operator_vesting.start_stage before performing the calculation, violating Pattern 3: Execution Boundaries and Validation Consistency.

vulnerabilities.title: Precision Loss in User Vesting Reward Calculation Due to Integer Division Truncation
vulnerabilities.description: The user vesting reward calculation uses integer division to compute vest_max_amount, which truncates fractional rewards. This causes systematic underpayment of users over time, with the lost funds accumulating in the vault without being distributed. The truncation occurs in create_user_vesting() when dividing initial_reward by (end_stage - start_stage), and no rounding or compensation mechanism exists.

vulnerabilities.title: Incomplete State Restoration in batch_claim_previous_user_vestings During Finalization
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_previous_user_vestings(), when a vesting is finalized (remaining_reward == 0), the function adds any remaining fractional reward (due to rounding) to net_vested_reward and sets remaining_reward to 0. However, this adjustment is not reflected in the UserVesting struct stored in the table. The struct's remaining_reward is already set to 0 during processing, but the additional reward added to net_vested_reward is never credited back to the struct before removal, causing a permanent accounting discrepancy.

vulnerabilities.title: Mathematical Domain Violation in mul_div_u64 with Zero Denominator
vulnerabilities.description: The utils::mul_div_u64 function is used in multiple places (e.g., batch_claim_previous_user_vestings, create_user_vesting) to compute proportional rewards. However, it is called with claim_info.total_l2_score as the denominator without checking if it is zero. If total_l2_score is zero, the function will abort due to division by zero, but this is not validated upstream. This causes transaction reverts during normal user interaction when no other users have L2 scores, effectively freezing reward distribution.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Type System Integrity - Mathematical Domain Validation

vulnerabilities.title: State Commitment Before External Call Validation in batch_claim_operator_reward
vulnerabilities.description: In batch_claim_operator_reward(), the last_claimed_stage is updated before the finalization loop completes. If the utils::walk_mut() loop fails (e.g., due to gas exhaustion or an unexpected revert), the last_claimed_stage is permanently advanced, preventing future claims on earlier stages. This commits state (last_claimed_stage) before verifying all operations succeeded, violating operation lifecycle integrity.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - State Commitment Timing

vulnerabilities.title: Authorization Context Binding Missing in Operator Vesting Claims
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_operator_reward function accepts claim_infos from any caller and uses operator_addr as the account identifier. However, there is no signature or authorization check binding the claim_infos to the operator_addr. An attacker can submit claim_infos for a different operator's vesting schedule, consuming the operator's last_claimed_stage and preventing legitimate claims. The authorization context (who is authorized to claim) is not bound to the data being claimed.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: Operation Lifecycle Integrity - Authorization Context Binding

vulnerabilities.title: Withdraw Function Allows Unlimited Withdrawals Without User Consent or Minimum Output Protection
vulnerabilities.description: The `withdraw` function allows any entity with knowledge of the vault's internal structure to withdraw any amount of funds without requiring user authorization or providing any mechanism for the user to specify a minimum acceptable output. This violates Pattern 1 (User Control Over Execution Outcomes) because users have no way to protect themselves against malicious or unfavorable withdrawals. The function reads the reward_per_stage value to validate that it is non-zero, but does not validate the withdrawal amount against any user-defined bounds, available balance, or reward accrual logic. This enables an attacker to drain the entire vault balance in a single call.

vulnerabilities.title: Validation of reward_per_stage Occurs After State Change in Withdraw Function
vulnerabilities.description: The `withdraw` function calls `primary_fungible_store::withdraw` to transfer funds out of the vault before validating that `reward_per_stage > 0`. This violates Pattern 2 (Validation Timing) because the state change (fund transfer) occurs before the validation check. An attacker can exploit this by setting `reward_per_stage` to 0 via `update_reward_per_stage` and then calling `withdraw` — the withdrawal will succeed because the validation occurs after the transfer, allowing funds to be stolen even when the protocol is supposed to be inactive.

vulnerabilities.title: Withdraw Function Bypasses Reward Accrual Logic and Allows Arbitrary Withdrawals
vulnerabilities.description: The `withdraw` function directly withdraws a specified amount from the vault without any relation to the `reward_per_stage` value beyond a zero-check. This violates Pattern 3 (Execution Boundaries and Validation Consistency) because the function's name and context imply it is meant to distribute rewards based on a per-stage rate, but it instead acts as a generic withdrawal function. This creates a critical accounting inconsistency: users expect withdrawals to be proportional to accrued rewards, but the function allows arbitrary withdrawals regardless of reward state. An attacker can withdraw 100% of the vault balance even if no rewards have been accrued, leading to fund theft.

vulnerabilities.title: update_reward_per_stage Allows Any Chain Signer to Set Reward to Zero, Enabling Fund Drain
vulnerabilities.description: The `update_reward_per_stage` function allows any entity holding the `chain` signer to set `reward_per_stage` to zero. This violates Pattern 5 (Conditional Recipient Selection) and Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing) because setting it to zero disables the reward mechanism but does not prevent withdrawals — which occur before validation. An attacker can call `update_reward_per_stage` with reward_per_stage=0, then immediately call `withdraw` to drain the entire vault. The state change (setting reward_per_stage=0) is committed before the withdrawal, but the withdrawal bypasses the validation, enabling a complete fund drain. This is a state commitment timing flaw: the state is modified to prevent future rewards, but the withdrawal logic still executes successfully.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: State Commitment Timing + Conditional Recipient Selection

vulnerabilities.title: No Access Control on Critical Functions in Public Interface
vulnerabilities.description: The `withdraw` function is public and can be called by any actor with knowledge of the vault's address and the ability to generate a valid signer for the vault's extend_ref. The `update_reward_per_stage` function is public and only requires a `chain` signer, which is not defined or restricted in the code. This violates Pattern 4 (Access Control in Interfaces) because critical functions that control fund movement and protocol parameters are exposed without access control modifiers or role-based restrictions. The interface design implies these functions are administrative, but no access control is declared, enabling any actor to manipulate the vault.

vulnerabilities.title: Withdraw Function Can Drain Vault Even If Balance Is Insufficient
vulnerabilities.description: The `withdraw` function does not check whether the vault's balance is sufficient to cover the requested withdrawal amount. It only checks that `reward_per_stage > 0`. This violates Pattern 3 (Execution Boundaries and Validation Consistency) and Pattern 7 (State Commitment Timing). If an attacker calls `withdraw(1000000)` when the vault holds only 100 tokens, the `primary_fungible_store::withdraw` call will revert — but this is not handled gracefully. However, if the underlying `primary_fungible_store` allows partial withdrawals or does not revert on insufficient balance (which is not guaranteed), the function could return a partial amount without updating the reward_per_stage or any accounting state. This creates an inconsistency: the caller receives less than requested, but the protocol does not track or adjust for this partial execution, leading to potential accounting drift or fund loss.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Metadata Is Hardcoded and Not Verifiable, Risking Interface Incompatibility
vulnerabilities.description: The `reward_metadata()` function returns a hardcoded metadata object for 'uinit' from @initia_std. This violates Pattern 8 (External System Assumptions) because the protocol assumes the existence and structure of a coin with symbol 'uinit' at @initia_std. If the external protocol changes the metadata structure, renames the coin, or deploys a fork with different semantics, the vault will interact incorrectly with the fungible asset system. This could cause deposits or withdrawals to fail silently, or worse, cause funds to be sent to an incorrect or non-existent asset type, resulting in permanent loss. There is no dynamic lookup or verification of the coin's existence or properties.

vulnerabilities.title: Withdrawal Funds Automatically Re-deposited via External System Returns
vulnerabilities.description: The vault contract has no mechanism to distinguish between user deposits and funds returned from external systems. When a withdrawal is executed via the withdraw() function, the funds are transferred from the vault's primary store to the caller. However, if those withdrawn funds are later sent back to the vault's address (e.g., via a misconfigured reward distribution, bridge refund, or malicious re-deposit), the deposit() function treats them as new user deposits. This causes the vault's balance to inflate artificially, and since reward_per_stage is applied to the total balance during future withdrawals, attackers can trigger inflationary reward distribution, effectively stealing from legitimate users by manipulating the fund source pool.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Reward Per Stage Update Allows Fee Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: The update_reward_per_stage function allows any account with chain permission to set the reward_per_stage value to any positive number. Since this value is used directly in the withdraw function to determine the amount of reward that can be withdrawn (without any scaling or accounting for deposited balance), an attacker can set reward_per_stage to an arbitrarily high value and withdraw all funds in the vault. This is a critical access control boundary violation because reward_per_stage is a core economic state variable that directly controls the withdrawal amount, yet it lacks any restriction to only authorized administrators or governance.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Withdrawal Bypasses Balance Constraints via Direct State Usage
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw function reads reward_per_stage directly and uses it as the withdrawal amount without any relation to the actual balance in the vault. This creates a representation boundary violation: reward_per_stage is intended to represent a per-stage reward rate (e.g., tokens per block or per epoch), but it is misused as an absolute withdrawal cap. Since the function does not check the vault's actual balance before withdrawing, an attacker can set reward_per_stage to 10^18 and withdraw the entire vault balance, even if only 1000 tokens were deposited. This is a critical unit mismatch — the variable is semantically a rate but is treated as an absolute amount.

vulnerabilities.title: Mathematical Proof: Attacker Can Drain Entire Vault with Single Manipulation
vulnerabilities.description: An attacker with chain permission can exploit the combination of update_reward_per_stage and withdraw to drain the vault. Step 1: Deposit 1000 uinit via deposit(). Step 2: Attacker calls update_reward_per_stage(vip, 1000000000000). Step 3: Attacker calls withdraw(1000000000000). The withdraw function does not validate that amount <= balance, and primary_fungible_store::withdraw will return up to the available balance (1000) even if requested amount is larger. However, since reward_per_stage is set to 1e12, the attacker can call withdraw multiple times (e.g., 1000 times with 1e9 each) to drain the entire 1000 uinit. Each withdrawal consumes the entire balance because the function does not reduce reward_per_stage or track cumulative withdrawals. The economic impact is total loss of all deposited funds to the attacker. Mathematical proof: After deposit(1000), balance = 1000. After update_reward_per_stage(1e12), withdraw(1e12) returns 1000. Attacker repeats 1 time and drains 1000 uinit. No mechanism exists to reset or cap withdrawals. Total loss: 100% of vault assets.
vulnerabilities.location: withdraw function, lines 44-49; update_reward_per_stage function, lines 58-65

vulnerabilities.title: No Accounting for Cumulative Withdrawals Enables Repeated Draining
vulnerabilities.description: The vault has no mechanism to track how much has been withdrawn or to reset reward_per_stage after withdrawal. This creates a data access integrity flaw: the reward_per_stage variable is treated as a mutable global cap, but it is never consumed or reset. An attacker can set reward_per_stage to a high value, withdraw once, then set it again to the same high value and withdraw again — effectively draining the vault multiple times. Even if the vault balance is zero, the withdraw function will still return the available balance (zero), but the attacker can re-set reward_per_stage to a high value and withdraw again if new deposits occur. However, if the attacker controls the chain permission, they can deposit funds themselves and then immediately withdraw them. This creates a circular drain: deposit -> update_reward_per_stage -> withdraw -> repeat. The data structure (reward_per_stage) is not synchronized with the vault balance, and no state tracks withdrawals, leading to indefinite exploitation potential.
vulnerabilities.location: withdraw function, lines 44-49; update_reward_per_stage function, lines 58-65

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Validation Bypass Allows Claiming Rewards for Non-Existent Scores
vulnerabilities.description: The get_merkle_root_and_proof function constructs a Merkle proof using a dummy hash for the complement score, but does not validate that the provided l2_score and total_l2_score are consistent with the actual snapshot data. An attacker can submit a snapshot with l2_score = 0 and total_l2_score = 0, yet provide a Merkle proof constructed as if total_l2_score > 0, and still pass validation. This allows claiming rewards for zero-score snapshots, effectively stealing rewards meant for other users. The vulnerability stems from the fact that the Merkle proof generation logic assumes the dummy hash is always valid, even when total_l2_score is zero, and the submit_snapshot function does not verify that the provided l2_score and total_l2_score match the actual state of the system.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Generation Allows Fabricated Rewards via Score Hash Collision
vulnerabilities.description: The get_merkle_root_and_proof function generates Merkle proofs using a deterministic hash construction that allows an attacker to submit a zero-score claim for a user while fabricating a valid Merkle proof for a non-zero reward. This occurs because the function constructs the Merkle proof using a dummy hash for the complement score (total_l2_score - l2_score), and the bytes_cmp function's lexicographic ordering allows an attacker to force the dummy hash to be placed first in the Merkle tree, making the proof valid even when l2_score = 0. This enables an attacker to claim rewards for zero contribution by submitting a zero-score snapshot with a forged proof, bypassing the intended reward distribution logic.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Claiming Allows Double-Spending via Re-registered Bridge Version Mismatch
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward_script and batch_claim_operator_reward_script functions do not validate that the bridge version in the claim request matches the current registered version of the bridge. An attacker can deregister a bridge, submit a snapshot with a high score, claim rewards using the old version, then re-register the bridge with a new version and claim the same rewards again under the new version. This exploits the fact that vesting positions are tracked by bridge_id and stage, not by bridge_id + version, allowing the same stage to be claimed twice under different versions. This results in double-spending of protocol rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Lock Staking Allows Theft of Vesting Rewards by Locking Non-Existent Positions
vulnerabilities.description: The lock_stake_script function allows users to lock stake any vesting position by stage number, even if that position was never claimed or does not exist. The function does not verify that the vesting position has been created via a prior claim. An attacker can submit a lock_stake_script call for a high stage number (e.g., 1000) with a large amount, causing the protocol to deduct that amount from the vault as if it were a legitimate vesting reward, even though no reward was ever generated for that stage. This results in direct theft of protocol funds from the vault.

vulnerabilities.title: Operator Reward Claiming Permits Unauthorized Claimants via Missing Caller Authorization
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_operator_reward_script function allows any caller to claim operator rewards for a bridge, without verifying that the caller is the currently registered operator for that bridge. The function only checks the bridge_id and version, but does not validate that the caller's address matches the operator address stored in the bridge registry. This allows any user to claim operator rewards intended for the legitimate operator, resulting in theft of operator rewards.

vulnerabilities.title: Partial Lock Staking Enables Reward Theft via Incomplete Vesting Finalization
vulnerabilities.description: The lock_stake_script function allows partial locking of vesting rewards, but does not properly account for the remaining unclaimed portion of the vesting position. When a user locks a portion of their vesting reward, the remaining amount is supposed to be forfeited as a penalty. However, the function does not update the vesting position's remaining reward to reflect the locked amount, and the penalty calculation in subsequent claim operations is based on the original initial reward, not the adjusted remaining. This allows an attacker to lock a large portion of a vesting reward, causing the protocol to incorrectly calculate a smaller penalty, effectively stealing the difference between the intended penalty and the actual penalty applied.

vulnerabilities.title: Zero Total Score Snapshots Allow Reward Manipulation via Division by Zero
vulnerabilities.description: The score_hash function and reward distribution logic do not properly handle cases where total_l2_score = 0. When total_l2_score is zero, the user's score ratio (l2_score / total_l2_score) becomes undefined, but the protocol still allows snapshot submission and reward calculation. In the reward distribution logic, this leads to division by zero in proportional calculations (e.g., when computing user share of pool rewards). Although the code may not explicitly divide by zero, the use of BigDecimal arithmetic with zero denominators in internal calculations can lead to undefined behavior, incorrect reward allocation, or silent underflow, allowing an attacker to manipulate reward distribution by submitting a snapshot with total_l2_score = 0 and a non-zero l2_score.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Reuse Enables Replay Attacks on Reward Claims
vulnerabilities.description: The protocol does not implement any replay protection for Merkle proofs. A valid Merkle proof generated for a specific stage and user can be reused in subsequent claim transactions for the same user and bridge, even after the reward has already been claimed. The batch_claim_user_reward_script function accepts the same merkle_proofs vector multiple times without checking whether the stage has already been claimed. This allows an attacker to replay a previously valid claim transaction and receive the same reward multiple times, leading to unlimited reward minting.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: State Commitment Timing and Replay Protection

vulnerabilities.title: Deregistered Bridge Reward Claims Allow Phantom Reward Extraction
vulnerabilities.description: After a bridge is deregistered, the protocol still allows users to claim rewards for snapshots submitted before deregistration. However, the reward distribution logic does not account for the fact that the bridge is no longer active, and the vault continues to pay out rewards based on outdated weights and TVL. An attacker can submit a snapshot with an artificially inflated score just before deregistration, then claim the reward after deregistration.
