Since the bridge is no longer registered, the protocol cannot update its state to reflect the invalidation of the claim, but the reward is still paid out from the vault. This results in permanent loss of protocol funds to attackers who exploit the deregistration timing window.
vulnerabilities.vulnerability_type: External System Assumptions and State Management

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Withdrawal Bypass via Zero Reward Per Stage
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw function requires reward_per_stage > 0, but this check is only enforced at withdrawal time. An attacker can set reward_per_stage to 0, deposit funds, then update reward_per_stage to a positive value and withdraw the full deposited amount without any reward logic being applied. This allows unauthorized extraction of deposited funds.
vulnerabilities.location: fun withdraw(amount: u64): FungibleAsset acquires ModuleStore

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Per Stage Update Allows Arbitrary Value Setting
vulnerabilities.description: The update_reward_per_stage function only checks that reward_per_stage > 0, but allows any positive u64 value to be set. This enables an attacker to set an astronomically high reward_per_stage value (e.g., 2^64 - 1), causing subsequent withdrawals to drain the entire vault balance in a single transaction, effectively enabling theft of all deposited funds.
vulnerabilities.location: public entry fun update_reward_per_stage(chain: &signer, reward_per_stage: u64) acquires ModuleStore

vulnerabilities.title: Missing Authorization Binding in Withdraw Function
vulnerabilities.description: The withdraw function uses a signer generated from the module's extend_ref, but does not bind the withdrawal amount or context to any caller authorization. Any entity that can call withdraw() (including malicious actors who obtain the extend_ref) can withdraw any amount, bypassing any intended access control. The function lacks any caller verification or signature binding.
vulnerabilities.location: public(friend) fun withdraw(amount: u64): FungibleAsset acquires ModuleStore

vulnerabilities.title: Insufficient Input Validation in Deposit Function
vulnerabilities.description: The deposit function only checks that amount > 0, but does not validate against maximum supply limits, vault capacity, or potential overflow conditions. An attacker could theoretically deposit amounts that cause arithmetic overflow in underlying storage or cause the fungible store to enter an invalid state, leading to funds being locked or corrupted.
vulnerabilities.location: public entry fun deposit(funder: &signer, amount: u64) acquires ModuleStore

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Metadata Hardcoded and Non-Configurable
vulnerabilities.description: The reward_metadata() function hardcodes the coin symbol as 'uinit' and uses a fixed metadata structure from @initia_std. If the external coin protocol changes its metadata schema (e.g., adds required fields like decimals, icon, or contract address), the interface becomes incompatible, causing all deposit/withdraw operations to revert due to ABI mismatch.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Claim and Lock Staking State Desynchronization Allows Double Reward Extraction
vulnerabilities.description: The protocol allows users to claim rewards and then lock-stake vesting positions, but the vesting position finalization logic does not properly account for the locked amount when calculating remaining rewards. This creates a state desynchronization where the same reward amount can be claimed multiple times through sequential lock-staking operations, effectively allowing users to extract more rewards than allocated by the protocol.

vulnerabilities.title: Unrestricted Snapshot Submission Allows Reward Manipulation via Stage Replay
vulnerabilities.description: The submit_snapshot and submit_snapshot_and_fund_reward functions allow any user to submit arbitrary snapshots with fabricated L2 scores and total scores, as long as they provide a valid Merkle proof. The Merkle proof generation is deterministic and publicly computable, and there is no access control restricting who can submit snapshots. This enables an attacker to replay old snapshots with inflated scores to claim disproportionate rewards. The vulnerability lies in the lack of access control on state-modifying functions that directly impact reward distribution, violating Access Control Boundary consistency. The attacker can manipulate the timing of snapshot submissions to exploit the vesting and reward distribution logic, effectively stealing rewards intended for legitimate users.

vulnerabilities.title: Merkle Proof Generation Uses Predictable Dummy Hash, Enabling Collusion and Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: The get_merkle_root_and_proof function generates Merkle proofs using a hardcoded dummy address (@0xff) and computes the dummy score as (total_l2_score - user_l2_score). This approach assumes that the dummy entry is always the complement of the user's score, but it does not verify that the dummy entry actually exists in the real data structure. An attacker can exploit this by submitting a snapshot with a total_l2_score of 0 and l2_score of 0, which generates a dummy hash of 0 and a Merkle root that is simply sha3_256(0 || 0). Since the system does not validate the existence or legitimacy of the dummy entry, an attacker can submit fake snapshots with zero scores and claim rewards as if they had contributed non-zero scores. This breaks the representation boundary between the logical score data and the cryptographic proof, allowing reward claims without actual contribution.

vulnerabilities.title: Vesting Position Finalization Logic Fails to Account for Deregistered Bridges, Enabling Reward Theft
vulnerabilities.description: When a bridge is deregistered, the system still allows users to claim rewards for snapshots submitted under that bridge. However, the vesting position finalization logic in lock_stake_script and batch_lock_stake_script does not check whether the bridge is still registered before finalizing vesting positions. This allows an attacker to deregister a bridge after users have claimed rewards, then submit new snapshots under the same bridge ID (after re-registration) with zero scores, and lock stake the previously claimed vesting positions. Since the vesting system does not invalidate positions tied to deregistered bridges, the attacker can effectively re-claim the same rewards multiple times by cycling between deregistration and re-registration. This violates Data Access Integrity because the vesting position state is not synchronized with the bridge registration state.

vulnerabilities.title: Reward Distribution Calculation Uses Unverified Total Score, Enabling Inflation Attack
vulnerabilities.description: The reward distribution logic in vip::fund_reward_script and vip::batch_claim_user_reward_script uses the total_l2_score provided in the snapshot to calculate the user's share. However, there is no mechanism to verify that the total_l2_score is consistent across all snapshots for a given stage. An attacker can submit multiple snapshots for the same stage with different total_l2_score values (e.g., 1000, 1000000), and the system will accept them all. When claiming rewards, the system uses the last submitted total_l2_score to compute the user's share, allowing the attacker to inflate the total score and claim a disproportionately large reward. This breaks the representation boundary between the intended total score (sum of all valid scores) and the submitted total score, leading to inflation of the reward pool and theft from other users.

vulnerabilities.title: Batch Claim Functions Do Not Validate Stage Continuity, Enabling Replay and Double-Spending of Rewards
vulnerabilities.description: The batch_claim_user_reward_script and batch_claim_operator_reward_script functions accept a vector of stages and corresponding Merkle proofs but do not verify that the stages are contiguous or in ascending order. An attacker can submit a list of stages that skips intermediate stages (e.g., [1, 3, 5]) and claim rewards for those stages without having claimed the rewards for stages 2 and 4. Since the vesting system tracks the last claimed stage per user, but the claim function does not enforce sequential progression, the attacker can replay old snapshots from earlier stages multiple times, effectively double-spending rewards. This violates Data Access Integrity because the iteration mechanism over the stages vector assumes completeness and ordering that are not enforced.
